content.thinking:
I need to double-check the timing discrepancy here—the flag change was recorded at 15:28:10 but the actual onset appears at 15:23, with logs showing the flag already active on most instances by then, suggesting the rollout may have happened gradually within that minute rather than at the logged change timestamp.

The person's account of manually rolling back the flag isn't corroborated by any change record, and Argus didn't take any automated action, so recovery around 15:28:27 seems to align with their claimed manual rollback even though it's unverified.

Building the causal chain now: roughly a third of account page traffic failed because requests hit a ZeroDivisionError in spend_summary.py, which only executed because the monthly-spend-feature flag flipped on. The division-by-zero root cause itself isn't explained by the evidence, so I'll stop there and focus on contributing factors—no staged rollout or guard—and recommend fixes like adding a division guard, testing, staged rollout with auto-rollback, and noting the roughly five-minute detection delay between onset and alert.

I also want to flag that the manual rollback wasn't captured in the change event record, so I'll add an action item for recording manual rollbacks or having Argus verify them. Then I'm numbering the action items in order: AI-1 for the division guard and test, AI-2 for staged flag rollout with auto-rollback, AI-3 for faster detection/alerting on error spikes, and AI-4 for process improvements around recording flag changes and rollbacks.

For the executive summary, I need to be careful with phrasing -- use placeholders like {duration}, {errors_while_broken}, and {errors_at_worst} rather than specific numbers or times, avoid writing exact timestamps or precise counts, and keep file/line references general rather than citing exact line numbers to stay safe.

action_items.item: Fix the division in the spend summary code in spend_summary.py to handle a zero divisor. Add a test for that case before the flag is enabled again.
Roll out feature flags in stages, such as a small percentage of traffic first. Gate each step on the account page error rate, and roll back automatically if it rises.
Add an alert on a spike in application exceptions such as ZeroDivisionError on io-shop. Tighten the error-rate alert so it pages soon after onset.

Make flag changes and rollbacks, including manual ones, appear in the change feed with accurate timestamps. Have Argus check the flag state and error rate after a human reports a rollback, before resolving.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers loading the account page got errors. The error rate rose from {errors_before} to {errors_while_broken} on average and peaked at {errors_at_worst}, for {duration}.
The failing requests raised ZeroDivisionError (division by zero) in the spend summary code in spend_summary.py. These errors began at the onset and continued until the end of the incident.

That code ran because the monthly-spend-feature flag went from off to on. Flag evaluations were off before the onset. At the onset most evaluations returned on, and afterwards all did. The change feed also records the flag being switched on by an admin.

The newly enabled path divides by a value that was zero for the affected requests. The record does not show why that value was zero or why the flag could be enabled without this being caught, so the chain stops here.

contributing_factors.factor: The spend summary code has no guard against a zero divisor, and nothing exercised that case before the flag went live.
The flag moved traffic to the new path quickly and with no staged rollout or automatic rollback on error rate, so a code bug reached a large share of traffic at once.
The alert was raised well after the failures began, so Argus and the responders started investigating late.

The change feed Argus read shows the flag being switched on, with a timestamp that does not line up with the onset. It shows no record of the manual rollback, so Argus could not confirm the cause or the fix from change data and left its leading candidate untried.

input.executive_summary: Account pages on the shop failed for a large share of shoppers for {duration}, starting at {began}. The error rate rose from {errors_before} to {errors_while_broken} on average and peaked at {errors_at_worst}. The failures started when a new feature flag, the monthly spend summary, was turned on and exposed a division-by-zero bug in the page's code. A person rolled the flag back by hand, and the metrics showed recovery at {recovered}. Argus's automated response made no change of its own. It moved to mitigating, then the person resolved the incident. The alert fired well after the failures began.

got_lucky: The fix was a single flag that could be reverted by hand, so no deploy or code change was needed to recover.
Latency, CPU and memory stayed flat, so the damage stayed limited to the account page path.
went_well: The Investigator Agent formed a candidate cause that matched the logs, naming the flag and the ZeroDivisionError.
A person rolled the flag back by hand, and the metrics recovered.
The log lines clearly tied the errors to the flag state.
went_wrong: The alert came well after the failures began, so shoppers were affected before anyone was paged.
Argus took no action of its own. The leading candidate was never tried, and recovery rested on a manual rollback it could not verify from the change feed.
The change event's time and the flag evaluation logs disagree about when the flag turned on, which clouds the timeline.

input.root_cause: Switching on the monthly-spend-feature flag sent account page requests down a spend-summary code path in spend_summary.py that divides by zero, so those requests raised ZeroDivisionError. The record does not show why the divisor was zero or why nothing guarded against it.
input.symptom: Account pages failed for many shoppers
